new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (19 pp., text layer, extracted text) and located the passage on PDF page 8 = printed p. 268 (footer 'Copyright IAARR 2013... 268'), immediately after Table 5 'Borrowings from English': 'Most technical expressions remain unchanged in English as in Tables 5(b) and are mostly maintained with the stress of the English Language without the tones of Agwagune being imposed on them. These include words such as menu, delete, laptop, software.' Verbatim match. grep of the full text confirms this is the only occurrence of 'stress' in the article; 'tone' occurs only here too, but all Agwagune data in Tables 1-5 carry H/L tone diacritics. The corroborating Huffman 1987 line is also verbatim in, s…
new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule for word-stress placement is stated by any source opened. Agwagune is described as a tone language (Huffman 1987; Ugot's data are marked with high/low tones and tonal alternations are described); Ugot 2013 contrasts native Agwagune tones with English stress, which is retained only on unassimilated English technical loans. Nothing says whether native words have a stress prominence at all.
new_statements.exceptions: Only that unassimilated English technical loans (menu, delete, laptop, software) keep English stress rather than receiving Agwagune tones (Ugot 2013: 268).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level; Ugot 2013 discusses isolated lexical items (loanwords); Huffman 1987 is an instrumental nasalization study of one Agwagwune speaker reading words in a frame sentence. Neither is a phonological description; the tone-language label is incidental in both.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources concern the prestige variety Agwagune/Agwagwune proper (Egip-Ipa clan, Biase LGA) = Glottolog agwa1247 'Nuclear Agwagwune'; Huffman 1987 records one speaker of 'Agwagwune'. The inaccessible Williams 2011 phonology describes the Adim dialect (Glottolog dialect under agwa1247; Ethnologue lists Adim as a dialect of Gwune), not the prestige variety.

sources.citation: Ugot, Mercy. 2014. Nominal plurality in Agwagune: a descriptive analysis. AFRREV LALIGENS 3(2): 66-88. DOI 10.4314/laligens.v3i2.5
sources.note: No mention of stress. p. 67 language background (Egip-Ipa clan, Biase LGA; Agwagune = central language of the Nne/Agwagune cluster: Agwagune, Erei, Adim, Abini, Etono II, Abayongo, Etono central); p. 70 plurality 'by tone' discussed for Niger-Congo generally (Ngiti), Agwagune plurals by vowel alternation/prefix; examples tone-marked.

sources.citation: Ugot, Mercy I. 2003 [CrossRef 2004]. Affixation in Agwuagune. Global Journal of Humanities 2(1&2): 28-31. DOI 10.4314/gjh.v2i1.29336
sources.note: Nothing on stress/accent. Tone remarks only: negative prefix /ge-/ 'always carries a high tone'; rising tones with lengthening in negation; elided vowel's 'plain low tone' merges with a following high tone; affixes trigger 'tonal alteration'.

sources.citation: Huffman, Marie K. 1987. Timing of contextual nasalization in two languages. UCLA Working Papers in Phonetics 69 (Coarticulation): 68-76.
sources.note: Sec. 2 Language Background, p. 68: 'The languages we are considering are both tone languages of West Africa.' p. 69: data from 'one speaker of Agwagwune, a little-studied language of Nigeria which has no oral/nasal contrast in vowels.' Nothing on stress or accent.
